source: These libraries conferred SpyCas9 resistance at levels 10-fold to 1,000-fold above background (Figure 1D).

claim: Plasmids containing contigs from Oral_5 and Fecal_01A had few escape mutations in Cas9 target sites.
source: Moreover, plasmids containing these contigs had few escape mutations in Cas9 target sites, so they likely withstood SpyCas9 due to functions encoded by their DNA inserts (Supplementary file 1 table S3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 1 table S3.

claim: Many contigs from Oral_5 and Fecal_01A were found to be phage-associated (30%).
source: Finally, many contigs from these libraries were found to be phage-associated (30%; Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1 table S4) and many encoded genes of unknown function (Figure 2—figure supplement 1); these are both hallmarks of known acrs (Borges et al., 2017; Pawluk et al., 2017a; Sontheimer and Davidson, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1 table S4.

claim: Many contigs from Oral_5 and Fecal_01A encoded genes of unknown function.
source: Finally, many contigs from these libraries were found to be phage-associated (30%; Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1 table S4) and many encoded genes of unknown function (Figure 2—figure supplement 1); these are both hallmarks of known acrs (Borges et al., 2017; Pawluk et al., 2017a; Sontheimer and Davidson, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Phage-association and encoding genes of unknown function are both hallmarks of known acrs.
source: Finally, many contigs from these libraries were found to be phage-associated (30%; Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1 table S4) and many encoded genes of unknown function (Figure 2—figure supplement 1); these are both hallmarks of known acrs (Borges et al., 2017; Pawluk et al., 2017a; Sontheimer and Davidson, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Borges et al., 2017, Pawluk et al., 2017a, and Sontheimer and Davidson, 2017.

claim: The contigs identified belonged to 19 bacterial genera.
source: The contigs identified belonged to 19 bacterial genera.
evidence: This is supported by taxonomic analysis presented in Supplementary file 1 table S4.

claim: Cas9 homologs are found in 15 of the 19 bacterial genera (79%) from which contigs were identified.
source: Intriguingly, Cas9 homologs are found in 15 of these 19 bacterial genera (79%, Supplementary file 1 table S4), a significant enrichment over the 12% of bacterial genera that harbor Cas9 (567/4822) in a representative set of ~24,000 bacterial genomes (Mendler et al., 2018) (p=8×10−20, χ² test).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 1 table S4 and comparison to data from Mendler et al., 2018.

claim: 12% of bacterial genera harbor Cas9 in a representative set of ~24,000 bacterial genomes.
source: Intriguingly, Cas9 homologs are found in 15 of these 19 bacterial genera (79%, Supplementary file 1 table S4), a significant enrichment over the 12% of bacterial genera that harbor Cas9 (567/4822) in a representative set of ~24,000 bacterial genomes (Mendler et al., 2018) (p=8×10−20, χ² test).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Mendler et al., 2018.

claim: The enrichment of Cas9-containing genera among recovered contigs is statistically significant (p=8×10−20, χ² test).
source: Intriguingly, Cas9 homologs are found in 15 of these 19 bacterial genera (79%, Supplementary file 1 table S4), a significant enrichment over the 12% of bacterial genera that harbor Cas9 (567/4822) in a representative set of ~24,000 bacterial genomes (Mendler et al., 2018) (p=8×10−20, χ² test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The enrichment of Cas9-containing genera strongly supports the hypothesis that many of the recovered contigs encode true acrs rather than artifacts of functional selection.
source: This enrichment strongly supports our hypothesis that many of the recovered contigs encode true acrs rather than artifacts of functional selection, since phages and MGEs must encounter Cas9 to benefit from the protective effect of acrs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical enrichment and biological reasoning.

claim: Upon individual re-testing, six oral and four fecal inserts protect a plasmid from SpyCas9.
source: Upon individual re-testing, six oral and four fecal inserts protect a plasmid from SpyCas9; p-values indicate comparisons to an empty vector in SpyCas9 inducing conditions and are adjusted for multiple hypotheses (Student's t-test, n = 3); + /- refers to SpyCas9 induction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Contig F01A_2 is from a Siphoviridae phage which lysogenizes Clostridium_Q sp.
source: Contig F01A_2 is from a Siphoviridae phage which lysogenizes Clostridium_Q sp.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The F01A_2 contig was the most abundant contig from the Fecal_01A library (with coverage 216-fold above the median coverage in the library).
source: Second, the F01A_2 contig was by far the most abundant contig from this library (with coverage 216-fold above the median coverage in the library), suggesting that it outperformed other contigs during selection.
evidence: This is supported by coverage data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: F01A_2 completely inhibited SpyCas9 activity.
source: In our re-testing, we confirmed that F01A_2 completely inhibited SpyCas9 activity (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: F01A_2 shares near-perfect nucleotide identity (>99.9%) with a Siphoviridae phage.
source: Finally, F01A_2 shares near-perfect nucleotide identity (>99.9%) with a Siphoviridae phage.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The Siphoviridae phage infects bacteria from the genus Clostridium_Q.
source: This phage infects bacteria from the genus Clostridium_Q, where it is found as a prophage in the genomes of some strains but not in those of close relatives (Figure 2C), suggesting that it is an actively circulating phage.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The Siphoviridae phage is found as a prophage in the genomes of some Clostridium_Q strains but not in those of close relatives, suggesting that it is an actively circulating phage.
source: This phage infects bacteria from the genus Clostridium_Q, where it is found as a prophage in the genomes of some strains but not in those of close relatives (Figure 2C), suggesting that it is an actively circulating phage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of prophage presence/absence shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Clostridium_Q is a member of the family Lachnospiraceae described recently in a reassessment of bacterial taxonomy.
source: Clostridium_Q is a member of the family Lachnospiraceae described recently in a reassessment of bacterial taxonomy (Parks et al., 2018) and includes the species Clostridium symbiosum, an important biomarker associated with colorectal cancer progression (Xie et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Parks et al., 2018.

claim: Clostridium_Q includes the species Clostridium symbiosum, an important biomarker associated with colorectal cancer progression.
source: Clostridium_Q is a member of the family Lachnospiraceae described recently in a reassessment of bacterial taxonomy (Parks et al., 2018) and includes the species Clostridium symbiosum, an important biomarker associated with colorectal cancer progression (Xie et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xie et al., 2017 and Thomas et al., 2019.

claim: The five open reading frames (ORFs) on F01A_2 are small, map to accessory regions of phage genomes, and appear to routinely undergo HGT.
source: As is typical for Acr-encoding loci, the five open reading frames (ORFs) on F01A_2 are small, map to accessory regions of phage genomes, and appear to routinely undergo HGT (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Orf_3 completely accounted for SpyCas9 inhibition: a null mutation in orf_3 reduced the frequency of KanR 105-fold, to the level of an empty-vector control.
source: Orf_3 completely accounted for SpyCas9 inhibition: a null mutation in orf_3 reduced the frequency of KanR105-fold, to the level of an empty-vector control (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Orf_3 was named acrIIA11.
source: This ORF, which we named acrIIA11, was sufficient for SpyCas9 antagonism, protecting a target plasmid (Figure 3B) from SpyCas9 approximately as well as acrIIA4, a potent inhibitor of SpyCas9 used in multiple gene-editing applications (Rauch et al., 2017; Shin et al., 2017; Basgall et al., 2018; Nakamura et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a naming decision by the authors.

claim: AcrIIA11 was sufficient for SpyCas9 antagonism, protecting a target plasmid from SpyCas9 approximately as well as acrIIA4.
source: This ORF, which we named acrIIA11, was sufficient for SpyCas9 antagonism, protecting a target plasmid (Figure 3B) from SpyCas9 approximately as well as acrIIA4, a potent inhibitor of SpyCas9 used in multiple gene-editing applications (Rauch et al., 2017; Shin et al., 2017; Basgall et al., 2018; Nakamura et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: AcrIIA4 is a potent inhibitor of SpyCas9 used in multiple gene-editing applications.
source: This ORF, which we named acrIIA11, was sufficient for SpyCas9 antagonism, protecting a target plasmid (Figure 3B) from SpyCas9 approximately as well as acrIIA4, a potent inhibitor of SpyCas9 used in multiple gene-editing applications (Rauch et al., 2017; Shin et al., 2017; Basgall et al., 2018; Nakamura et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rauch et al., 2017, Shin et al., 2017, Basgall et al., 2018, and Nakamura et al., 2019.

claim: SpyCas9 with a non-targeting crRNA allows Mu phage to successfully infect E. coli.
source: When SpyCas9 is equipped with a non-targeting crRNA that does not recognize Mu's genome, the phage successfully infects E. coli.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: SpyCas9 with a Mu-targeting crRNA robustly inhibits phage infection when no Acr is present.
source: However, when SpyCas9 contains a Mu-targeting crRNA, its expression robustly inhibits phage infection, provided that no Acr is present.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: When either acrIIA11 or acrIIA4 is expressed, SpyCas9 immunity is nearly completely abolished.
source: When either acrIIA11 or acrIIA4 is expressed, SpyCas9 immunity is nearly completely abolished, confirming the ability of these Acrs to inhibit SpyCas9 and restore phage infection (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: AcrIIA11 bears no discernible homology to any previously identified acr.
source: AcrIIA11 bears no discernible homology to any previously identified acr (Borges et al., 2017; Pawluk et al., 2017a; Lee et al., 2018; Uribe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and citations to previous work.

claim: Many proteins homologous to AcrIIA11 were identified in both phage and bacterial genomes.
source: We identified many proteins homologous to AcrIIA11 in both phage and bacterial genomes and focused on a high-confidence set of homologs, those with ≥35% amino acid identity that cover ≥75% of AcrIIA11's 182 amino acid sequence (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence database searches and analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: AcrIIA11 homologs have a wider phylogenetic distribution than most previously identified type II-A anti-CRISPRs.
source: AcrIIA11 homologs have a wider phylogenetic distribution than most previously identified type II-A anti-CRISPRs (Figure 4A) and span multiple bacterial phyla (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1 table S5).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: AcrIIA11 homologs span multiple bacterial phyla.
source: AcrIIA11 homologs have a wider phylogenetic distribution than most previously identified type II-A anti-CRISPRs (Figure 4A) and span multiple bacterial phyla (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1 table S5).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and data in Supplementary file 1 table S5.

claim: AcrIIA11 homologs clustered into three monophyletic groups.
source: We made a phylogenetic tree of AcrIIA11 homologs and found that they clustered into three monophyletic groups (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: AcrIIA11 homologs from each group were identified in a variety of MGEs.
source: AcrIIA11 homologs from each group were identified in a variety of MGEs (Figure 4C), consistent with our observation that AcrIIA11 routinely undergoes HGT (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis shown in Figure 4C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The three groups on the AcrIIA11 phylogenetic tree correspond directly to the three bacterial taxonomic clades in which AcrIIA11 is found.
source: Despite these signatures of HGT, the three groups on the AcrIIA11 phylogenetic tree (Figure 4B) correspond directly to the three bacterial taxonomic clades in which AcrIIA11 is found (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4A, Figure 4B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: While HGT of acrIIA11 may readily occur across short phylogenetic distances, intra-class and intra-phylum gene flow is rare.
source: This concordance between gene and species clusters indicates that, while HGT of acrIIA11 may readily occur across short phylogenetic distances, intra-class and intra-phylum gene flow is rare, in contrast to what has been observed for some other acrs (Uribe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic analysis, with citation to Uribe et al., 2019 for comparison.

claim: Type II-A CRISPR-Cas systems are enriched in the Lachnospiraceae relative to other bacterial families (p=5×10−27, χ² test).
source: Type II-A CRISPR-Cas systems are enriched in the Lachnospiraceae relative to other bacterial families (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, p=5×10−27, χ² test), which suggests that MGEs in these bacteria regularly encounter type II-A systems.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of genomic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The enrichment of type II-A CRISPR-Cas systems in Lachnospiraceae suggests that MGEs in these bacteria regularly encounter type II-A systems.
source: Type II-A CRISPR-Cas systems are enriched in the Lachnospiraceae relative to other bacterial families (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, p=5×10−27, χ² test), which suggests that MGEs in these bacteria regularly encounter type II-A systems.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical enrichment.

claim: All tested AcrIIA11 homologs in the 'a' group inhibited SpyCas9.
source: This could explain why all tested AcrIIA11 homologs in the 'a' group (Figure 4B) inhibited SpyCas9 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Two genes from the 'a' group, acrIIA11a.1 and acrIIA11a.2, are found within 2 Kb of a putative aca4 homolog.
source: Consistent with their anti-CRISPR activity, two genes from this group, acrIIA11a.1 and acrIIA11a.2, are found within 2 Kb of a putative aca4 homolog (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), which has been previously associated with multiple acr loci (Marino et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A and citation to Marino et al., 2018.

claim: Aca4 has been previously associated with multiple acr loci.
source: Consistent with their anti-CRISPR activity, two genes from this group, acrIIA11a.1 and acrIIA11a.2, are found within 2 Kb of a putative aca4 homolog (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), which has been previously associated with multiple acr loci (Marino et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Marino et al., 2018.

claim: Aca-linked loci often encode hot spots of multiple acrs.
source: Because aca-linked loci often encode hot spots of multiple acrs (Pawluk et al., 2016b; Borges et al., 2017; Pawluk et al., 2017a), we also tested 17 genes from these loci for their capacity to inhibit SpyCas9 in a plasmid protection assay.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pawluk et al., 2016b, Borges et al., 2017, and Pawluk et al., 2017a.

claim: None of the 17 genes flanking acrIIA11a.1 and acrIIA11a.2 encoded strong inhibitors of SpyCas9.
source: We found that none of these genes encoded strong inhibitors of SpyCas9 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B and C), although it remains possible that they exhibit anti-CRISPR activity – perhaps against type I-C or III-A systems, as many of the tested genes are found in prophages which encounter these CRISPR-Cas subtypes (e.g. in Ruminococcus_B lactaris, NCBI accession QSQN01).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B and C.

claim: It remains possible that genes flanking acrIIA11a.1 and acrIIA11a.2 exhibit anti-CRISPR activity against type I-C or III-A systems.
source: We found that none of these genes encoded strong inhibitors of SpyCas9 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B and C), although it remains possible that they exhibit anti-CRISPR activity – perhaps against type I-C or III-A systems, as many of the tested genes are found in prophages which encounter these CRISPR-Cas subtypes (e.g. in Ruminococcus_B lactaris, NCBI accession QSQN01).
evidence: This is speculation based on the genomic context of these genes.

claim: Very few Acrs have been mechanistically characterized.
source: Considering their relatively recent discovery, it is not surprising that very few Acrs have been mechanistically characterized.
evidence: This is an inference based on the state of the field.

claim: AcrIIA2 and AcrIIA4 are dsDNA mimics that inhibit SpyCas9 by binding to its gRNA-loaded form and preventing association with a dsDNA target.
source: Nonetheless, a common theme has emerged from biochemical studies of AcrIIA2 and AcrIIA4, the only type II-A Acrs for which a mechanism of Cas9 inhibition has been elucidated. These studies have shown that both AcrIIA2 and AcrIIA4 are dsDNA mimics; they inhibit SpyCas9 by binding to its gRNA-loaded form and preventing association with a dsDNA target (Dong et al., 2017; Shin et al., 2017; Yang and Patel, 2017; Jiang et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dong et al., 2017, Shin et al., 2017, Yang and Patel, 2017, Jiang et al., 2019, and Liu et al., 2019.

claim: Untagged AcrIIA11 migrates at approximately twice its predicted molecular weight by size exclusion chromatography, suggesting that it may function naturally as a dimer.
source: We first observed that untagged AcrIIA11 migrates at approximately twice its predicted molecular weight by size exclusion chromatography (Figure 5A), suggesting that it may function naturally as a dimer.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Purified AcrIIA11 inhibited the dsDNA cleavage activity of SpyCas9 in-vitro, in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Consistent with its ability to protect plasmids and phage from SpyCas9 in vivo, purified AcrIIA11 inhibited the dsDNA cleavage activity of SpyCas9 in-vitro, in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: AcrIIA11 is sufficient for SpyCas9 inhibition and does not require additional host or phage factors, at least in vitro.
source: These data demonstrate that AcrIIA11 is sufficient for SpyCas9 inhibition and does not require additional host or phage factors, at least in vitro.
evidence: This is an inference from the in vitro cleavage assay data.

claim: AcrIIA11's autonomous activity is consistent with its phylogenomic signature, as it shows no linkage to any other gene across phage genomes.
source: This autonomous activity is consistent with acrIIA11's phylogenomic signature, as it shows no linkage to any other gene across phage genomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is an inference based on genomic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: AcrIIA11 did not prevent SpyCas9 from binding a single-guide RNA (sgRNA).
source: AcrIIA11 did not prevent SpyCas9 from binding a single-guide RNA (sgRNA) and we did not observe a strong AcrIIA11/sgRNA interaction (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A strong AcrIIA11/sgRNA interaction was not observed.
source: AcrIIA11 did not prevent SpyCas9 from binding a single-guide RNA (sgRNA) and we did not observe a strong AcrIIA11/sgRNA interaction (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: AcrIIA11 limited migration of the SpyCas9/sgRNA ribonucleoprotein through a native gel, suggesting that AcrIIA11 may bind this complex.
source: Notably, AcrIIA11 did limit migration of the SpyCas9/sgRNA ribonucleoprotein through a native gel, suggesting that AcrIIA11 may bind this complex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: AcrIIA11 was unable to bind the I-SmaMI meganuclease (used as a negative control).
source: We found that AcrIIA11 was unable to bind the I-SmaMI meganuclease (used as a negative control) but bound both the apo (without sgRNA) and sgRNA-loaded forms of SpyCas9.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: AcrIIA11 bound both the apo (without sgRNA) and sgRNA-loaded forms of SpyCas9.
source: We found that AcrIIA11 was unable to bind the I-SmaMI meganuclease (used as a negative control) but bound both the apo (without sgRNA) and sgRNA-loaded forms of SpyCas9.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The addition of sgRNA enhanced AcrIA11 binding to SpyCas9.
source: The addition of sgRNA enhanced AcrIA11 binding to SpyCas9 (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2) but to a lesser extent than previously documented for both AcrIIA2 and AcrIIA4 (Dong et al., 2017; Shin et al., 2017; Yang and Patel, 2017; Jiang et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The addition of sgRNA enhanced AcrIA11 binding to SpyCas9 to a lesser extent than previously documented for both AcrIIA2 and AcrIIA4.
source: The addition of sgRNA enhanced AcrIA11 binding to SpyCas9 (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2) but to a lesser extent than previously documented for both AcrIIA2 and AcrIIA4 (Dong et al., 2017; Shin et al., 2017; Yang and Patel, 2017; Jiang et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work, supported by citations.

claim: Both AcrIIA2 and AcrIIA4 prevent sgRNA-complexed SpyCas9 from binding target dsDNA.
source: Both AcrIIA2 and AcrIIA4 have the key property of preventing sgRNA-complexed SpyCas9 from binding target dsDNA (Dong et al., 2017; Shin et al., 2017; Yang and Patel, 2017; Jiang et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dong et al., 2017, Shin et al., 2017, Yang and Patel, 2017, Jiang et al., 2019, and Liu et al., 2019.

claim: AcrIIA4 prevents the gel-shift caused by SpyCas9/sgRNA binding to its target dsDNA.
source: Consistent with previous work (Dong et al., 2017; Shin et al., 2017; Yang and Patel, 2017), we found that AcrIIA4 prevents the gel-shift caused by SpyCas9/sgRNA binding to its target dsDNA (Figure 6A, lane 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and citations to previous work.

claim: AcrIIA11 does not prevent the gel-shift caused by SpyCas9/sgRNA binding to its target dsDNA, even at molar ratios that abolish SpyCas9 cleavage activity.
source: In contrast, we observe that AcrIIA11 does not prevent this gel-shift, even at molar ratios that abolish SpyCas9 cleavage activity (compare lanes 2 through 5; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: AcrIIA11 creates a super-shifted SpyCas9/sgRNA/dsDNA ternary complex.
source: Instead of preventing a SpyCas9-induced gel-shift, we see that AcrIIA11 creates the opposite effect, giving rise to a super-shifted SpyCas9/sgRNA/dsDNA ternary complex (lane 4, Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A similar super-shift occurs using both short and long dsDNA substrates.
source: A similar super-shift occurs using both short and long dsDNA substrates, which differ in the amount of dsDNA unprotected by SpyCas9's footprint and thus exposed to AcrIIA11 (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: AcrIIA11 binds SpyCas9 to trigger the super-shift.
source: Because the shorter substrate has minimal dsDNA overhangs (five bp), AcrIIA11 binding to adjacent dsDNA is not likely to result in the super-shift observed; instead, we conclude that AcrIIA11 binds SpyCas9 to trigger this super-shift (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: AcrIIA11 retards the migration of apo-, sgRNA-loaded, and dsDNA-bound SpyCas9 through a native gel in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Consistent with this model, we observe that AcrIIA11 retards the migration of apo-, sgRNA-loaded, and dsDNA-bound SpyCas9 through a native gel in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: AcrIIA11 binds a motif on SpyCas9 preserved across all three conformations of the enzyme.
source: These data suggest that AcrIIA11 binds a motif on SpyCas9 preserved across all three conformations of the enzyme.
evidence: This is an inference based on the binding data.

claim: AcrIIA11 binding to a motif preserved across SpyCas9 conformations distinguishes it from AcrIIA2 and AcrIIA4, which bind to the dsDNA binding site of SpyCas9 only available in its sgRNA-loaded form.
source: This also distinguishes AcrIIA11 from AcrIIA2 and AcrIIA4, which bind to the dsDNA binding site of SpyCas9 only available in its sgRNA-loaded form (Dong et al., 2017; Shin et al., 2017; Yang and Patel, 2017; Jiang et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work, supported by citations.

claim: AcrIIA11 binds dsDNA weakly in the absence of SpyCas9.
source: In addition to binding SpyCas9, AcrIIA11 binds dsDNA weakly in the absence of SpyCas9 (lanes 8 and 9, Figure 6A), but strongly in the presence of either apo- or sgRNA-loaded SpyCas9 (compare 'band #2' in lanes 4 and 12 with 8 and 11, Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: AcrIIA11 binds dsDNA strongly in the presence of either apo- or sgRNA-loaded SpyCas9.
source: In addition to binding SpyCas9, AcrIIA11 binds dsDNA weakly in the absence of SpyCas9 (lanes 8 and 9, Figure 6A), but strongly in the presence of either apo- or sgRNA-loaded SpyCas9 (compare 'band #2' in lanes 4 and 12 with 8 and 11, Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: SpyCas9 does not co-migrate with 'band #2', confirming that AcrIIA11 binds dsDNA to generate this gel-shift.
source: We verified this behavior by Western blot, demonstrating that SpyCas9 does not co-migrate with 'band #2', thereby confirming that AcrIIA11 binds dsDNA to generate this gel-shift (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: AcrIIA11 undergoes a conformational change that enhances its dsDNA-binding upon interaction with SpyCas9.
source: Based on these findings, we hypothesize that AcrIIA11 undergoes a conformational change that enhances its dsDNA-binding upon interaction with SpyCas9.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: A Coomassie-stained native gel shows that AcrIIA11 forms a discrete, bright band in the presence of SpyCas9 but is more diffuse in its absence, indicating that SpyCas9 may stabilize a conformation of AcrIIA11.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, a Coomassie-stained native gel shows that AcrIIA11 forms a discrete, bright band in the presence of SpyCas9 but is more diffuse in its absence (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), indicating that SpyCas9 may stabilize a conformation of AcrIIA11.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: AcrIIA11 does not bind single-stranded DNA.
source: In contrast to our result with dsDNA, we do not detect binding of AcrIIA11 to single-stranded DNA (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: AcrIIA11 can directly bind multiple conformations of SpyCas9.
source: In summary, we demonstrate that AcrIIA11 can directly bind multiple conformations of SpyCas9 and that SpyCas9 induces AcrIIA11 to bind dsDNA.
evidence: This is a summary of the biochemical findings.

claim: SpyCas9 induces AcrIIA11 to bind dsDNA.
source: In summary, we demonstrate that AcrIIA11 can directly bind multiple conformations of SpyCas9 and that SpyCas9 induces AcrIIA11 to bind dsDNA.
evidence: This is a summary of the biochemical findings.

claim: It is uncertain which of AcrIIA11's behaviors (SpyCas9 binding, dsDNA binding, or both) contribute to SpyCas9 antagonism.
source: Though our results leave uncertain which of these behaviors, in isolation or combination, contribute to SpyCas9 antagonism, they make clear that AcrIIA11 uses a different mechanism of inhibiting SpyCas9 than the dsDNA mimicry employed by AcrIIA2 or AcrIIA4.
